strengths: Well-motivated problem: Effectively demonstrates that existing metrics give high scores to semantically incorrect reconstructions (e.g., teddy bear→cat), a genuine practical issue in visual brain decoding

Rigorous analysis of existing evaluation schemes: Systematic criticism of current metrics identifying dependency on comparison pool, lack of difficulty in two-way identification tasks, and misalignment with human perception

Solid empirical validation: Human evaluation on 1,000 image pairs with meta-evaluation using multiple metrics (pairwise accuracy 81.0% vs EffNet 78.0%); comprehensive worst-case analysis showing complementary component strengths
Interpretable metric components: Object F1 (object detection), Cap-Sim (caption similarity), and EffNet are human-understandable, providing transparency vs. pure embedding-based approaches
Practical utility: Pairwise hinge loss shows consistent improvements across three different models (MindEye2, MindBridge, UniBrain); loss is compatible with existing MSE-based training objectives
Comprehensive experimental analysis: Evaluation across multiple decoding models and discovery of semantic near-miss phenomenon (15-21% rate), demonstrating model limitations beyond high metric scores
Reproducibility and community contribution: Open-sourcing human judgment data provides valuable resource; implementation code provided; experimental details included
weaknesses: Limited novelty of individual components: Object F1 is straightforward threshold-averaged F1, Cap-Sim is simple caption similarity, and EffNet is existing work; main contribution is their combination via averaging, which is relatively incremental

Simplistic combination strategy: SEED = (Object F1 + Cap-Sim + EffNet) / 3 lacks justification; no exploration of learned weighting, adaptive combination, or comparison with alternative aggregation methods
Insufficient inter-rater reliability analysis: No Cohen's kappa or Fleiss' kappa reported; no analysis of evaluator disagreement or treatment of outliers; unclear if 22 evaluators is sufficient

Limited scope of human evaluation: Ratings only from MindEye2-generated reconstructions and 4 NSD subjects, raising questions about generalization to other decoding models and subjects—critical limitation for a universal metric

Concerning EffNet component choice: Table 2 shows EffNet exhibits extreme behavior (same-class: +0.755 vs human +0.313; different-class: -0.333 vs human -0.138); including a biased metric undermines the stated goal of human alignment

Object F1 limitations underexplored: Limited to 82 categories; misses semantic content not in object lists (acknowledged in Fig. 4a with global scene failure); fine-grained distinctions problematic; ablation on location/size/number (Table 4) suggests fundamental limitations

Cap-Sim single model dependency: Relies on GIT for captions with no sensitivity analysis; caption generation quality and model-specific biases not explored; example in Fig. 4b shows struggles with gender/attribute changes

Pairwise hinge loss is incremental: Straightforward order-preservation constraint; modest improvements (Table 3 shows 0.5-2% gains, some <1%); SEED improvement from 0.474 to 0.475 is likely within noise; no statistical significance testing
No statistical rigor in evaluation: No confidence intervals, significance tests, or error bars reported; is 81.0% vs 78.0% statistically significant with 1,000 samples?

Incomplete experimental reproducibility for loss validation: Authors reduced latent space to 1024 and removed low-level pipeline due to computational constraints, meaning baselines don't perfectly match originals; hyperparameter search details incomplete
Acknowledged perceptual limitation not addressed: Authors admit SEED ignores perceptual aspects; semantic correctness ≠ visual quality; provides incomplete solution to evaluation problem
Model dependency and longevity concerns: Metric relies on fixed pretrained models (MM-Grounding-DINO, GIT, EffNet) that may become outdated; no robustness analysis to model updates

Missing ablations: No exploration of weighted combinations, caption model sensitivity, or justification for why averaging is optimal vs. excluding biased EffNet component (Object F1+EffNet achieves 80.1%, only 0.9% below SEED)

strengths: Well-motivated problem with compelling examples (teddy bear → cat). Effectively demonstrates misalignment between existing metrics and human judgment.
Substantial human evaluation effort: 1,000 image pairs × 22 annotators provides valuable validation data and reproducible resource for the community.

Comprehensive empirical analysis including multiple correlation measures, systematic comparison of 12 existing metrics, insightful worst-case judgment analysis, and quantification of semantic near-miss phenomenon (17-20%).
Practical improvements demonstrated across three different decoding models (MindEye2, MindBridge, UniBrain) with reproducible implementation.
Improved interpretability compared to pure embedding-based metrics through object and caption components.
weaknesses: Limited novelty of core contribution: SEED simply averages three existing/straightforward components (Object F1, Cap-Sim, EffNet). No novel metric design; purely an engineering combination without principled justification.

Oversimplified metric combination: Uses naive averaging without exploring learned weights, alternative aggregation schemes, or principled framework. Table 5 shows Object F1+EffNet (80.1%) nearly matches SEED (81.0%), questioning necessity of all components.

Inconsistent criticism: Paper criticizes existing metrics for relying on pre-trained models, yet SEED equally depends on MM-Grounding-DINO, GIT, and EffNet. 'Interpretability' claim is overstated—these are still deep learning models.

Severely limited scope: Single dataset (NSD), only 4 subjects, only diffusion-based models evaluated. No cross-dataset validation or generalization analysis. Human data comes only from MindEye2 reconstructions.

Human evaluation limitations: No inter-annotator agreement metrics reported. Asks for both 'semantic and perceptual' similarity simultaneously (may be conflated). Coarse 5-point Likert scale. No confidence intervals or significance testing on correlation improvements.
Cap-Sim concerns: Highly vulnerable to caption generation errors from GIT. No ablation on caption model choice. May introduce systematic biases from hallucinations or semantic drift.

Object F1 limitations: Restricted to 82 categories missing many concepts. Cannot capture quantities ('one dog' vs. 'many dogs'), spatial relationships, or fine-grained attributes. Ablation (Table 4) shows size/location/number information don't help, suggesting metric is too coarse.
Incomplete problem-solving: Paper identifies 17-20% semantic near-miss rate but proposes no solution. Doesn't address fundamental limitations of object-based and caption-based evaluation.

Pairwise hinge loss contribution is modest: Improvements <1% in many cases (Table 3). Standard ranking loss technique without novel insights. Different hyperparameters needed per model suggests potential overfitting.

Limited statistical rigor: No confidence intervals, significance testing, or cross-validation. No analysis of metric sensitivity to image category, reconstruction quality, or dataset composition. Robustness claims insufficient.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: Existing evaluation metrics show near-perfect performance despite semantic errors, creating a genuine need for better metrics
Rigorous human evaluation study with 1,000 GT-reconstruction pairs and 22 evaluators, using multiple meta-evaluation metrics (pairwise accuracy, Kendall's Tau-b, Pearson correlation)
SEED demonstrates consistent improvements over existing metrics (81.0% vs 78.0% pairwise accuracy over EffNet; 0.621 vs 0.559 Kendall's Tau)

Well-motivated combination of complementary metrics: Object F1 for object presence, Cap-Sim for semantic attributes, EffNet for style/scene information; empirically validated that combinations of existing metrics alone cannot achieve this improvement
Insightful analysis including worst-case judgment examples (Fig. 4), quantification of semantic near-miss phenomenon (17.5-20.6%), and discovery of EffNet's class-bias
Strong reproducibility: human evaluation data to be released, clear experimental details, Python implementation provided, comprehensive hyperparameter documentation
Practical applicability: pairwise hinge loss broadly compatible with multiple existing methods and consistently improves performance across models
Clear presentation with effective motivation, well-organized structure, and illuminating figures
weaknesses: Limited component novelty: Object F1 is straightforward application of existing object detection, Cap-Sim uses off-the-shelf caption models, EffNet is pre-existing; main novelty is combining them
SEED uses simple equal-weight averaging without principled justification or exploration of learned/optimized weights despite heatmap suggesting potential variations

Limited scope of human evaluation: only 1,000 pairs, 22 evaluators provide limited diversity, only 4 subjects, human ratings collected only on MindEye2 reconstructions raises question of generalization to other models' outputs
Insufficient analysis of component dependencies: no robustness testing to failure modes of MM-Grounding-DINO, GIT, or Sentence Transformers; reproducibility depends on external models that may change
Metric design choices lack justification: why 82 specific object categories, threshold averaging scheme (Eq. 3) is non-standard, limited ablation studies
Pairwise hinge loss improvements are modest: <0.01 improvements on most metrics, inconsistent effects on low-level metrics, tested only on 3 related models from similar labs
Perceptual aspects explicitly excluded (colors, textures, fine details) despite relevance to brain decoding quality assessment
Experimental setup changes from original MindEye2 (1024 vs 4096 dims, removed low-level pipeline) justified by informal 'advice from author' rather than principled reasoning
Cross-dataset validation missing: only Natural Scenes Dataset evaluated; generalization to other brain imaging datasets unclear
Statistical significance testing absent in Table 1; no inter-rater reliability statistics (e.g., Fleiss' kappa) provided

strengths: Well-motivated problem identifying genuine misalignment between existing metrics and human judgment in visual brain decoding
Rigorous human evaluation with 1,000 image pairs from 22 evaluators (ICC=0.84) providing solid empirical foundation
Comprehensive robustness analysis across multiple datasets, models, and off-the-shelf component choices with consistent strong performance
Actionable failure mode analysis revealing semantic near-miss phenomenon (17.5-20.6%) and semantic detail misses (8.3-10.7%) with clear guidance for model improvement
SEED achieves statistically significant improvement over best existing metric (81.0% vs 78.0% pairwise accuracy) with proper statistical testing
Thorough ablation studies and supplementary analyses in appendix demonstrating careful experimental design
Reproducibility commitment with code and human evaluation data to be released, enabling future research
Clear, well-written presentation with interpretable metric components inspired by visual perception stages
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: metric combines existing components (object detection, image captioning, EffNet) in straightforward manner; individual novelty (Cap-Sim) is conceptually simple
Simple averaging combination lacks principled justification; no exploration of learned weights or more sophisticated combination strategies despite heterogeneous metrics
Object F1 design concerns: fixed 82-category vocabulary limits applicability, single highest-confidence object per category is arbitrary, no distinction between salient and background objects
Cap-Sim shows sensitivity to caption generation quality with failures when similar images generate descriptively different captions (e.g., action differences)
SEED fails on common model outputs (distorted/malformed images) undermining claims of human-alignment for typical brain decoding failures
Evaluation scope is limited: only 2 datasets (NSD with 4 subjects, GOD with 50 images), 2 decoding models tested; unclear generalization across subjects and stimulus types
Neuroscience motivation regarding two-stage visual attention is interesting but loosely connected to actual metric design involving semantic/linguistic processing
Improvements over best baseline (EffNet) are modest at ~3% pairwise accuracy; practical significance for model development decisions unclear
SEED inherits systematic errors from component models (MM-Grounding-DINO, GIT, Sentence Transformer); sustainability concern as these models evolve
Threshold-averaging approach in Eq. 3 lacks theoretical justification; computational cost not discussed; alternative combination strategies not explored despite C.1 ablations

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Clearly demonstrates misalignment between current metrics and human judgment with concrete examples
Comprehensive empirical evaluation: Multiple meta-evaluation metrics, multiple datasets/models, statistical significance testing, and robustness analysis across component choices
Valuable human evaluation resource: 1,000 images × 22 raters (ICC=0.84) will benefit the research community; code and data planned for release
Honest treatment of limitations: Transparently discusses SEED's failure modes and error sources; acknowledges limitations in design choices
Insightful diagnostic analysis: Identifies specific failure modes (semantic near-miss at 17.5-20.6%, detail-miss at 8.3-10.7%) across multiple models
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: Core contribution is averaging three existing/straightforward methods without learned weighting or principled fusion strategy. Object F1 is straightforward object detection application; Cap-Sim is trivial cosine similarity; EffNet is reformulated existing metric

Weak theoretical justification: Connection between neuroscience-inspired two-stage attention and actual metric design is loose and post-hoc. No justification for equal weighting; Table 5 shows different combinations perform differently but weighted alternatives unexplored

Insufficient component analysis: Object F1 has limited category set (82 classes), fails on fine-grained distinctions (Fig. 11a: Sink vs. Toilet); Cap-Sim highly sensitive to caption quality and linguistic variation; no ablation studies justifying component choices
No proposed solutions for identified problems: Paper identifies failure modes but provides only vague speculation as remedies. Thresholds for categorizing failures are somewhat arbitrary
Limited evaluation scope: Only 2 datasets tested (NSD + 50-image GOD subset); only 5 recent models evaluated; no evaluation on broader model range or image types; GOD evaluation is minimal

Practical limitations inadequately addressed: Three-model pipeline introduces computational cost (not analyzed) and error propagation; Fig. 10 shows complete failure when all components fail simultaneously on distorted images
Modest empirical improvements in some metrics: SEED improves from 78.0% to 81.0% pairwise accuracy over EffNet—statistically significant but practically modest; other metrics show smaller gains

Incomplete statistical analysis: Bootstrap only varies evaluators, not images; conflation of semantic and perceptual similarity in human ratings; no analysis of rating consistency across evaluator subgroups
Limited baseline comparisons: No comparison to other semantic similarity metrics (LPIPS, modern CLIP-based approaches); VQA approach underperforms but not thoroughly investigated

Unclear generalization: Will SEED apply beyond brain decoding? Could metric be optimized specifically to this human evaluation dataset? How will it handle different failure mode distributions in future models?

strengths: Well-motivated problem identifying real gaps between existing metrics and human judgment in visual brain decoding
Valuable human evaluation dataset (1,000 images, 22 evaluators, ICC=0.84) with commitment to release
Neuroscience-inspired design grounded in two-stage visual attention theory
Rigorous meta-evaluation with multiple metrics, cross-dataset validation, and statistically significant improvements with bootstrapped CIs
Robust to choice of off-the-shelf models (grounding, captioning, embedding) with minimal performance variance
Actionable failure mode analysis quantifying semantic near-miss (17.5-20.6%) and detail miss (8.3-10.7%) phenomena
Clear presentation with effective figures, detailed methodology, and reproducibility commitment
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: simple unweighted averaging of three existing/established methods with no principled justification for equal weighting
Marginal empirical improvements: only +0.9% pairwise accuracy over Object F1+EffNet (81.0% vs 80.1%), raising questions about practical benefit over simpler combinations
Fundamental brittleness from component model dependencies: all three metrics can simultaneously fail on distorted/unusual images, precisely when evaluation is most needed
Narrow scope limited to image reconstruction from fMRI; untested on text decoding, other modalities, or non-object-centric images
Object F1 uses fixed 82 categories checking only existence without spatial relationships, number, or attributes; VLM variant performs worse
Cap-Sim sensitivity to caption quality with no robust error handling; single caption per image inadequate for ambiguous semantics
Limited human evaluation scale and consistency: 22 total evaluators, inconsistent protocols across datasets, only 50 images for GOD dataset
Missing comparisons to other semantic similarity metrics (LPIPS, DINO, etc.); restricted to 8 metrics from brain decoding literature
Arbitrary thresholds in failure mode definitions lack sensitivity analysis
Statistical analysis concerns: bootstrapping on only 22 evaluators may yield overly optimistic confidence intervals
